basics.name: Angel Ollin Patricio
basics.label: Incoming M.Eng. Student, MIT EECS
basics.summary: Incoming MIT MEng student passionate about interpretability, alignment, and theory of deep learning. Background spans distributed PyTorch for decentralized ML, LLM evals, and learning dynamics of language and vision models; most recently, mechanistic interpretability of RL-induced reward hacking in LLMs.

work.name: Solar-Lezama Group, MIT CSAIL
work.summary: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding with Origami
highlights: Extended an existing Gymnasium MDP formulation of inverse origami for language model evaluation, writing tooling to automate benchmark generation from a curated set of 25 reusable target origami stored as .obj files. Acknowledged in the OrigamiBench writeup.

Established baseline shape-reconstruction performance by comparing MCTS, PPO, random walks, and evolutionary methods against the preliminary benchmark suite. Found strong correlation between performance drop and shape complexity in all approaches except random.

work.name: Camera Culture Group, MIT Media Lab
work.summary: SONAR Web: Real-Time Decentralized Learning Across Heterogeneous Edge Clients
highlights: Built cross-platform federated learning clients in Python (PyTorch) and JavaScript (TensorFlow.js). Leveraged a platform-agnostic config format and a universal JSON-based weight representation for framework-agnostic communication between heterogeneous peers.

Contributed to a WebRTC communication layer with a central-server handshake for session join and zero server involvement thereafter. Implemented chunked streaming weight transfer to share larger models between peers, bypassing WebRTC's 16MB data channel limit.

Validated cross-platform training and weight exchange across ring, mesh, toroidal, and Erdős-Rényi topologies with up to 12 peers, verifying gradient flow on MLP and CNN baselines over MNIST and CIFAR. Core components remain in the published system.

work.name: Edelman Lab, MIT IMES
highlights: Rebuilt data pipeline for DistilBERT fine-tuning on the 30M-sample CELLxGENE census dataset, writing custom collators for the transcriptomics format including both sharding and streaming to eliminate full-dataset memory pressure. Parallelized training with HF accelerate across 8+ GPUs on a Vast.ai instance, cutting epoch times from hours to minutes.

Built automation with WandB logging, allowing full experiment suites producing a collection of masked language modeling checkpoints, trained over vectors of concatenated phenotype labels and 500+ dimensional gene expression profiles. This formulation allowed a single model to perform classification, imputation, or both depending on the masking pattern; deployed a simple Streamlit interface for inference on user samples.

projects.name: Mechanistic Interpretability Testbed for Reward Hacking in Qwen3-4B
highlights: Extended the reproducible RL-induced reward hacking setup from ariahw/rl-rewardhacking for Qwen3-4B into an expandable testbed for mechanistic interpretability tools to study how reward hacking emerges in language models; implemented activation caching over rollouts via PyTorch forward hooks.
Still ongoing, and serves as a live testbed for trying out different mechanistic interpretability tools as I learn the landscape of the field ahead of grad school.

Building in stages: training linear probes on residual-stream activations to detect hacking vs. honest behavior at prompt time, and implementing activation patching to localize the responsible components and steering along probe directions to suppress hacking.

projects.name: Finding an Edge of Stability for LLM Post-Training
projects.summary: Course project, MIT 6.7960 Deep Learning (Fall 2025; revisited 2026)
highlights: Built a PyTorch/HF pipeline tracking global and batch sharpness (top Hessian eigenvalues via PyHessian) while fine-tuning Pythia models (70M to 1.4B) on Alpaca with full SFT and LoRA, searching for the Edge of Stability (EoS) in LLM post-training. Initial experiments found no EoS signature.

Revisited the project in 2026 after finding flaws in the original measurements: rebuilt curvature tooling GPU-native in PyTorch (Hessian-vector products, batched power iteration) for a ~5× speedup over the CPU-bound original; validated against exact Hessians on small models, reference-library solvers, and invariant checks.

Established a positive control with the new tooling, confirming existing EoS results, but did not observe EoS in the full-scale experimental runs (up to 1.4B): sharpness built up early, then slowly tapered off instead of settling at a stability threshold, and near-degenerate top eigenvalues made single-eigenvalue estimates unstable. Archived.
